query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced ethanol oxidation performance in high-entropy PGM catalysts is governed by the catalyst’s promotion of hydrogen spillover from active sites to an adjacent reducible support, which accelerates the removal of poisoning intermediates and maintains active sites.
generation.material_initial_state: A platinum-group metal-based high-entropy alloy catalyst initially supported on a conventional carbon substrate with minimal hydrogen spillover capability.
generation.intervention: Replace the inert carbon support with a reducible oxide support (e.g., TiO2 or CeO2) without altering the catalyst’s metal composition or loading.
generation.conditions: Ethanol oxidation performed under identical electrochemical conditions (same temperature, electrolyte, and applied potential) in a fuel-cell-like setup.
generation.structural_mediator: The interface between the PGM sites and the reducible oxide support that facilitates hydrogen spillover, enabling active hydrogen atoms to transport to the support and oxidize adsorbed carbonaceous species.
generation.mechanism: Dissociative adsorption of hydrogen at the PGM sites generates atomic hydrogen, which migrates onto the reducible support. This hydrogen spillover aids in the oxidation and removal of strongly-bound intermediates that would otherwise poison the active sites, thereby promoting the full 12-electron, 12-proton oxidation of ethanol.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts on reducible supports will exhibit higher turnover frequencies, reduced accumulation of poisoning intermediates (as tracked in-situ using FTIR or isotopic labeling), and demonstrably enhanced long-term durability compared to those on inert carbon.
generation.baseline: Catalyst supported on conventional carbon with limited hydrogen spillover ability.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold only when the support is actively reducible. On non-reducible supports, hydrogen spillover is minimal and no enhancement is observed.
generation.uncertainty: Although hydrogen spillover has been well documented on reducible oxides and correlated to improved catalytic performance in related systems, the absolute quantitative contribution in ethanol oxidation remains to be rigorously established. However, the supporting evidence from PMC8222268 and PMC6203812 confirms the viability of this mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy PGM catalysts; one supported on a reducible oxide (e.g., TiO2) and the other on inert carbon. Monitor ethanol oxidation activity while simultaneously recording in-situ FTIR spectra for adsorbed intermediates and performing isotopic labeling experiments to track hydrogen migration.
measurements: Electrochemical activity (current density, onset potential, long-term stability)
In-situ FTIR spectroscopy to quantify accumulated adsorbed intermediates
Isotopic labeling (e.g., using D2) to detect hydrogen spillover kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If switching to a reducible support does not result in decreased poisoning (as evidenced by similar in-situ adsorbate signatures) or enhanced catalytic performance relative to the carbon-supported catalyst, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Hydrogen spillover is the term used to describe the migration of activated H atoms from noble metal NPs to the surfaces of the metal oxides on which they are supported. This phenomenon has applications in the fields of hydrogen storage materials, sensor fabrication, and heterogeneous catalysis., Hydrogen spillover is favored on reducible transition metal oxides such as TiO2, CeO2, and WO3 because active H atoms are able to migrate over oxide surfaces as proton (H+)/electron (e–) pairs based on the reaction Mn+ + O2– + H → M(n–1)+ + OH–. Our group previously demonstrated that NPs made of binary solid-solution alloys having non-equilibrium compositions (specifically, Ru–Ni and Rh–Cu) can be synthesized by utilizing individual H atoms originating from hydrogen spillover as a strong reductant to promote the simultaneous rapid reduction of deposited metal cations at low temperatures.− This prior work also involved the synthesis of CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs with a mean diameter of 2 nm, in which there are large gaps between the reduction potentials of the constituent elements, using the pronounced hydrogen spillover effect of TiO2. The development of new catalysts with simultaneously enhanced activity and selectivity is always the ultimate goal of researchers. In heterogeneous catalysis, the screening of new catalyst can be simply guided by the Sabatier principle. It indicates that the best catalysts should bind reactive intermediates with suitable interaction strength: neither too strong that leads to surface poisoning, nor too weak which fails to activate the reactants. The principle behind this phenomenon can be attributed to the existence of scaling properties of adsorption energies on transition metal surfaces, and various linear scaling relationships have been developed which connect the reaction energy/barriers with binding energy of representative surface species, i.e., descriptors. Therefore, the complicated reaction kinetics can be described by only a few descriptors, which enables fast screening of potential catalytic materials with the help of density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been intensively pursued as potentially advanced materials because of their exceptional properties. However, the facile fabrication of nanometer-sized HEAs over conventional catalyst supports remains challenging, and the design of rational synthetic protocols would permit the development of innovative catalysts with a wide range of potential compositions. Herein, we demonstrate that titanium dioxide (TiO2) is a promising platform for the low-temperature synthesis of supported CoNiCuRuPd HEA nanoparticles (NPs) at 400 °C. This process is driven by the pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on TiO2 in conjunction with coupled proton/electron transfer. The CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs on TiO2 produced in this work were found to be both active and extremely durable during the CO2 hydrogenation reaction. Characterization by means of various in situ techniques and theoretical calculations elucidated that cocktail effect and sluggish diffusion originating from the synergistic effect obtained by this combination of elements.Subject terms: Catalyst synthesis, Heterogeneous catalysis, Porous materials Facile fabrication of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) nanoparticles

We succeeded in the facile low-temperature synthesis of supported HEA NPs, taking advantage of the hydrogen spillover that proceeds on TiO2 via a coupled proton–electron transfer mechanism. Both in situ observations and theoretical simulations provided evidence that Pd2+ ions are first reduced by H2 to generate nuclei, after which the dissociation of hydrogen molecules occurs to form active hydrogen atoms that enable the simultaneous reduction of neighboring precursors. A CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 catalyst synthesized in this manner exhibited different selectivity and significantly improved stability compared with Pd/TiO2 during the hydrogenation of CO2. Theoretical investigations also emphasized that the sluggish diffusion in these CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs is caused by the combination of multiple metals, and that lattice distortion plays a crucial role in the superior robustness of this material. The preliminary H2-TPR studies of the quinary-component precursors including Rh, Pt, and Au on TiO2 generated only a single reduction peak (Supplementary Fig. 19), which is suggestive of the formation of HEA NPs by the simultaneous reduction of the mixed-metal precursors.
